description: A solo explorer analyzing the cosmos. Armed with Python code and a passion for astrophysics, I am independently tackling the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. My mission is to turn raw coordinate data into clear, visual maps to spot hidden anomalies moving across the night sky.
summary: Stars stand still. Strangers move. NASA's SPHEREx telescope photographs the whole sky in 102 infrared colors and comes back to the same patches again and again. If you flip between two pictures of the same patch, anything that moved, like an asteroid, a nearby brown dwarf, or maybe even a hidden distant planet, seems to jump out. We built an explainer page with a small blink game, a Python program that finds movers by comparing two visits, and a plan for a free public tool that does this with real SPHEREx images. Our demo sky is simulated, and we say so.
details:
Space was a childhood thing for me. When I was younger I never really understood why people liked to study it. This challenge changed that a little, because it asked a question I could actually picture: how do you spot something that moves in a sky full of things that stay still?

What I made: a project page, a short Python program, and a plan for a free public tool that lets anyone watch the sky change over time. The page explains SPHEREx and Planet X in plain words and has a small game. You blink between two pictures of a sky and click the dots that jump. The program, sky_blink.py, does the same job in code. It compares two visits to the same patch of sky, removes the stars that did not move, and reports what is left and how fast it went.

How it would work with real data: pick a patch of sky, pull its SPHEREx images from NASA/IPAC IRSA, and compare images of similar color, because SPHEREx sees each star through a different color in each exposure and a fixed star can look brighter or fainter. Then blink or subtract the visits, and check the suspects against Gaia DR3 (stars already known to move) and NEOSSat and the Canadian Astronomy Data Centre (asteroids and satellites).

Why it matters: the challenge resources say WiseView has helped the public make hundreds of discoveries, and SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months. More eyes could find more. I wanted something anyone can try without installing software.

What is real and what is not: the demo sky and the sample results are simulated, and I say so on the page and on the pictures. I did not connect the project to real SPHEREx images, and the Gaia option in my code is written but not tested with live data. I am not claiming to have found Planet X. Nobody has.

Tools: Python (csv, math, random, matplotlib), HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and GitHub.

Use of AI: the debugging Python code and the project page were written with the help of an AI assistant, Claude, by Anthropic.
dataRefs: SPHEREx at NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive
